questions.question: What does perplexity measure for a language model?
options: exp of the average per-token negative log-likelihood; lower is better
The share of multiple-choice questions answered correctly; higher is better
How many tokens per second the model generates at inference
The number of model parameters divided by the vocabulary size
questions.explanation: Perplexity = exp(mean cross-entropy loss per token). Lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to the real text. It is only comparable between models that use the same tokenization.

source.title: Hugging Face, Perplexity of fixed-length models

questions.question: Two models with different tokenizers report perplexity on the same text. Why can't the numbers be compared directly?
options: Perplexity is identical for every model evaluated on the same text
Perplexity changes with the GPU the model runs on
It is per token, and the tokenizers split the text differently
Perplexity can only be computed for image models
questions.explanation: Perplexity averages over tokens, and token boundaries differ between vocabularies, so the values are on different scales. Per-character or per-byte measures (e.g. bits per byte) or downstream tasks allow fair comparison.

source.title: Hugging Face, Perplexity of fixed-length models

questions.question: Which metric was designed for machine translation and is based on modified n-gram precision with a brevity penalty?
options: Mean reciprocal rank
ROUGE
BLEU
Perplexity
questions.explanation: BLEU compares n-gram overlap between candidate and reference translations, emphasizing precision, and penalizes outputs that are too short. ROUGE is recall-oriented and used mainly for summarization.

source.title: Papineni et al., BLEU: a Method for Automatic Evaluation of Machine Translation

questions.question: Which metric family is most commonly used to evaluate automatic summarization against reference summaries?
options: ROUGE (recall-oriented n-gram overlap)
Perplexity of the reference summary
BLEU (precision with a brevity penalty)
Accuracy on a confusion matrix
questions.explanation: ROUGE (e.g. ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L) measures how much of the reference content appears in the generated summary. It is the standard automatic summarization metric, although it misses paraphrases.

source.title: Lin, ROUGE: A Package for Automatic Evaluation of Summaries

questions.question: Generated answers are correct but phrased differently from the references, so BLEU and ROUGE scores are low. Which metric better captures semantic similarity?
options: Character-level edit distance
ROUGE-2 bigram overlap
BERTScore (contextual embedding similarity)
Exact match after lower-casing and removing punctuation
questions.explanation: BERTScore matches tokens using contextual embedding similarity, so paraphrases score well. N-gram metrics reward only surface overlap. LLM-as-a-judge is another option for semantic evaluation.

source.title: Zhang et al., BERTScore: Evaluating Text Generation with BERT

questions.question: For extractive question answering (e.g. SQuAD), which two metrics are standard? (Select two.)
options: Exact Match (EM)
Mean squared error
Perplexity of the question
BLEU-4 with brevity penalty
Token-level F1 between predicted and reference answers
questions.explanation: SQuAD-style QA uses Exact Match (strict string equality after normalization) and token-overlap F1 (partial credit). BERT, for example, reported SQuAD Test F1.

source.title: Devlin et al., BERT (SQuAD results)

questions.question: A team wants to compare models on broad academic knowledge across 57 subjects, from STEM to the humanities. Which benchmark fits?
options: SQuAD
GSM8K
HumanEval
MMLU
questions.explanation: MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) is multiple-choice questions over 57 subjects. HumanEval tests code generation, GSM8K grade-school math and SQuAD reading comprehension.

source.title: Hendrycks et al., Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding

questions.question: Which benchmark evaluates code generation by running unit tests on generated Python functions, reported as pass@k?
options: MMLU
HumanEval
GLUE
TruthfulQA
questions.explanation: HumanEval contains hand-written programming problems with unit tests. pass@k is the probability that at least one of k sampled solutions passes. It measures functional correctness, not text similarity.

source.title: Chen et al., Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code (HumanEval)

questions.question: GLUE and SuperGLUE are best described as:
options: Suites of GPU performance tests for training throughput
Suites of image generation tasks scored by panels of human raters
Suites of language understanding tasks with one aggregate score
Suites of code generation tasks scored with unit tests
questions.explanation: GLUE bundles several NLU tasks (e.g. MNLI, SST-2, QQP) into one score. SuperGLUE followed with harder tasks after models saturated GLUE. BERT famously pushed the GLUE score to 80.5%.

source.title: Wang et al., GLUE: A Multi-Task Benchmark and Analysis Platform for NLU

questions.question: Match the benchmark to what it measures. Which two pairs are correct? (Select two.)
options: GSM8K: multi-step grade-school math word problems
HumanEval: commonsense completion of everyday sentences
HellaSwag: correctness of generated Python functions under unit tests
TruthfulQA: whether models avoid common misconceptions
MMLU: image classification accuracy across 57 visual categories
questions.explanation: GSM8K is math word problems and TruthfulQA measures truthfulness against common falsehoods. HellaSwag is commonsense sentence completion, MMLU multi-subject knowledge and HumanEval code generation.

source.title: Lin et al., TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods

questions.question: A team wants to run many standard academic benchmarks (e.g. HellaSwag, ARC, MMLU) on a Hugging Face model with few-shot settings and reproducible scripts. Which open-source tool is built for this?
options: EleutherAI LM Evaluation Harness
Weights & Biases Sweeps
Triton perf_analyzer
NeMo Curator quality classifiers
questions.explanation: The LM Evaluation Harness is a framework for few-shot evaluation of language models, with 60+ standard benchmarks, configurable few-shot settings and many backends (HF, vLLM, APIs).

source.title: EleutherAI, lm-evaluation-harness

questions.question: A model tops a public leaderboard but performs poorly on the company's own support tickets. What is the best conclusion?
options: Assume the company's tickets are labeled incorrectly
Switch to a bigger model without further evaluation
Build a task-specific evaluation set from real tickets
Trust the leaderboard and keep the model unchanged
questions.explanation: Benchmarks measure general abilities and may be contaminated or mismatched with your task. A golden set of real, representative examples with the metrics that matter is the reliable basis for choosing a model.

source.title: NVIDIA DLI, Evaluating RAG and Semantic Search Systems

questions.question: Which bias of LLM-as-a-judge is mitigated by swapping the order of the two answers and averaging the verdicts?
options: Sampling bias in the training data
Position bias
Tokenization bias
Survivorship bias
questions.explanation: LLM judges tend to favour an answer because of its position (often the first). Evaluating both orders and requiring consistency reduces this. Judges also show verbosity bias and self-enhancement bias.

source.title: Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena

questions.question: A team uses an LLM to grade the quality of chatbot answers. Which two practices make the judge more trustworthy? (Select two.)
options: Run the judge at a high temperature to explore opinions
Always use the same model as both the chatbot and the judge without checks
Give the judge a clear rubric and, ideally, reference answers
Check agreement between the judge and human ratings on a sample
Prefer the longest answer automatically
questions.explanation: Rubrics and references reduce ambiguity, and validating against human labels shows whether the judge can be trusted. Self-judging risks self-enhancement bias, length preference is a known bias, and high temperature adds noise.

source.title: Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena

questions.question: In RAG evaluation, what does faithfulness (groundedness) measure?
options: Whether the answer addresses the user's actual question
Whether the retrieved documents are the most recent ones
Whether the retriever responds within the latency budget
Whether the answer's claims are supported by the context
questions.explanation: Faithfulness checks that every claim in the answer can be inferred from the provided context, which detects hallucination. Answer relevancy measures whether the answer addresses the question, and context precision/recall measure retrieval.

source.title: Es et al., RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation

questions.question: A RAG answer is fully supported by the retrieved passages but doesn't answer what the user asked. Which metric flags this?
options: Faithfulness
Answer relevancy
Index build time
Embedding dimension
questions.explanation: The answer is faithful to the context but irrelevant to the question. Answer relevancy evaluates whether the response addresses the user's question. Both metrics are needed, because each catches a different failure.

source.title: Es et al., RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation

questions.question: A query has 4 relevant documents in the corpus. The retriever's top 5 results contain 2 of them. What is recall@5?
options: 0.4 (2 of the 5 results are relevant)
0.5 (2 of the 4 relevant documents were retrieved)
1.0 (at least one relevant document was retrieved)
0.8 (4 relevant documents for 5 result slots)
questions.explanation: Recall@k = relevant documents found in the top k ÷ all relevant documents = 2/4 = 0.5. Precision@5 would be 2/5 = 0.4. 'At least one relevant in the top k' is hit rate@k, which is a different metric.

source.title: Evaluation measures (information retrieval): recall, precision@k

questions.question: For three queries, the first relevant document appears at ranks 1, 2 and 4. What is the mean reciprocal rank (MRR)?
questions.explanation: MRR averages 1/rank of the first relevant result per query: (1 + 0.5 + 0.25)/3 = 0.583. It rewards putting a relevant document near the top.

source.title: Evaluation measures (information retrieval): mean reciprocal rank

questions.question: Relevance labels are graded (0 = irrelevant, 1 = partly, 2 = highly relevant) and the team wants a ranking metric that rewards placing highly relevant documents first. Which fits best?
options: Hit rate@k
Mean reciprocal rank
nDCG
Recall@k
questions.explanation: nDCG uses graded relevance and discounts gains logarithmically by rank, normalized against the ideal ordering. Hit rate and plain recall treat relevance as binary.

source.title: Evaluation measures (information retrieval): nDCG

questions.question: A RAG system gives wrong answers. To find out whether retrieval or generation is at fault, which two measurements should the team take separately? (Select two.)
options: The vector database's license type and its maximum collection size
Generation quality given the context, e.g. faithfulness and correctness
GPU temperature and power draw on the inference server during the test
The number of words and the reading level of the system prompt
Retrieval quality, e.g. recall@k against a golden set of relevant chunks
questions.explanation: Evaluating the components separately localizes the failure. If the right chunks aren't retrieved, fix chunking, embeddings or the search. If they are retrieved but the answer is wrong or unfaithful, fix the prompt or the model.

source.title: Es et al., RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation

questions.question: A team changes the chunk size, the embedding model and the prompt at the same time, and accuracy improves by 6 points. What is the main problem with this experiment?
options: Accuracy is not a valid metric for RAG systems
Three variables changed, so the gain can't be attributed
Prompts should never be changed during experiments
A 6-point gain is always statistically insignificant
questions.explanation: Good experiment design changes one factor at a time, or uses a factorial design, with everything else fixed, so the effect can be attributed. Otherwise the team doesn't know which change helped or whether one change hurt.

source.title: Weights & Biases Docs, Quickstart (tracking experiments)

questions.question: An LLM-based classifier scores 82% on one run and 79% on a rerun with identical settings and temperature 0.7. Before claiming that a new prompt (83%) is better, what should the team do? (Select two.)
options: Run each configuration several times and compare the means and variance
Report only the best run of each configuration to keep things simple
Use a larger test set so the estimate is less noisy
Switch evaluation metrics until the new prompt comes out ahead
Accept the single 83% run as proof, since it beats both earlier runs
questions.explanation: Sampling makes results noisy, and a 1-3 point difference may just be run-to-run variance. Repeated runs, confidence intervals or significance tests and larger evaluation sets give trustworthy comparisons.

source.title: Weights & Biases Docs, Quickstart (tracking experiments)

questions.question: Two chatbot prompts are tested in production by randomly assigning users to version A or B and comparing task-completion rates. What is this?
options: Cross-validation
An A/B test
Data augmentation
Knowledge distillation
questions.explanation: An A/B test randomizes real users between variants, so differences in outcomes can be attributed to the variant. It needs enough traffic for statistical significance and a pre-defined success metric.

source.title: Google ML Crash Course, Production ML systems: monitoring and testing

questions.question: Why use an experiment tracker such as Weights & Biases or MLflow during fine-tuning experiments?
options: To replace the validation set with live dashboards of training loss
To speed up the GPU kernels used during training
To log configs, metrics and artifacts so runs are reproducible
To tokenize and cache the dataset before training
questions.explanation: Trackers record each run's configuration, loss curves, evaluation metrics and model artifacts, so teams can compare runs, reproduce results and spot regressions. They don't change model performance by themselves.

source.title: Weights & Biases Docs, Quickstart

questions.question: When tuning several hyperparameters with a limited budget, why is random search often more efficient than grid search?
options: It needs no evaluation metric to compare the different trials
It tries more distinct values of the parameters that matter
It tests every combination, just in a random order
It always finds the global optimum in fewer trials
questions.explanation: With a grid, many trials reuse the same values of the parameters that matter. Random search explores more distinct values of each dimension for the same number of trials, which usually finds good settings faster.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Tuning the hyper-parameters of an estimator

questions.question: A team keeps tweaking prompts and hyperparameters while checking results on the test set after every change. What is the risk?
options: They underfit, because the test set is too small to learn from
The test set grows larger each time it is used for checks
They overfit to the test set, so its score becomes optimistic
There is no risk: tuning on the test set is its purpose
questions.explanation: Repeatedly selecting configurations by test performance turns the test set into a validation set. Use a separate validation (dev) set for tuning and touch the held-out test set only for the final estimate.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Cross-validation

questions.question: A team must choose between two LLMs of similar quality for a high-volume product. Besides quality, which two factors should their evaluation include? (Select two.)
options: Release date, since newer is always better
Cost per request or per million tokens at the expected volume
How many languages the vendor's website supports
Parameter count, since bigger is always better
Latency and throughput on the target hardware
questions.explanation: Evaluating emerging technologies means weighing cost, performance (latency, throughput), portability, compatibility and licensing alongside quality. These decide whether a model is viable at production scale.

source.title: NVIDIA, NCA-GENL exam objectives (Experimentation)

questions.question: Before launch, a team wants to know how many concurrent users their LLM service can support within a 2-second latency target. What kind of test is this?
options: An accuracy benchmark such as MMLU on the target GPU
A unit test that checks one function with fixed inputs
A regression test on a golden set of expected answers
A load test that ramps up concurrency and measures latency
questions.explanation: Load testing, for example with perf_analyzer or a load generator, ramps up concurrent requests and records latency percentiles and throughput to find the capacity limit. Accuracy benchmarks don't measure capacity.

source.title: Triton perf_analyzer README

questions.question: After every prompt change, a team reruns a fixed set of 100 representative questions with expected behaviours and compares the results with the previous version. What is this practice?
options: Load testing at peak concurrency
Hyperparameter search on the test set
Regression testing on a golden set
A/B testing with live users
questions.explanation: A golden set acts as a regression suite. Running it on every change shows whether quality improved or broke something that used to work. It is the LLM-app equivalent of automated tests in software engineering.

source.title: NVIDIA DLI, Evaluating RAG and Semantic Search Systems

questions.question: What are the main limitations of BLEU and ROUGE for evaluating chatbot answers? (Select two.)
options: They can only be computed on GPUs with large amounts of memory
Valid paraphrases can score low because the wording differs
They measure inference speed and latency rather than output quality
They need a human judge to score every single example by hand
Fluent but factually wrong answers can still score well
questions.explanation: N-gram overlap metrics are cheap and reproducible but measure surface word overlap, not meaning or factual correctness. For open-ended generation they are complemented by embedding metrics, LLM judges and human evaluation.

source.title: Zhang et al., BERTScore: Evaluating Text Generation with BERT

questions.question: When is human evaluation most valuable in an LLM project?
options: Only for measuring latency and throughput under load
Only for counting tokens to estimate the API bill
Never, because automatic metrics are always sufficient
For subjective quality and to validate automatic metrics
questions.explanation: Humans judge nuance that metrics miss and provide ground truth for calibrating LLM judges. Their ratings are also the preference data used in RLHF and DPO. It is costly, so it is used strategically.

source.title: Ouyang et al., Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

questions.question: The top 10 retrieved chunks for a query contain 3 relevant chunks. What is precision@10?
options: It can't be computed without the total number of relevant documents
questions.explanation: Precision@k = relevant results in the top k ÷ k = 3/10 = 0.3. Precision doesn't need the total number of relevant documents in the corpus, whereas recall@k does.

source.title: Evaluation measures (information retrieval): precision@k

questions.question: Why is a learning-rate warmup often used at the start of Transformer training?
options: It makes the final model smaller and faster to serve
Ramping up from a small rate stabilizes early training
It removes the need for a separate validation set
Starting from a high rate helps escape poor initial weights
questions.explanation: Large updates at the very start, when Adam's moment estimates are poor and weights are random, can destabilize training. The original Transformer increased the learning rate linearly for the first warmup steps and then decayed it.

source.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (Sec. 5.3, Optimizer)
